title: Zahlen und Buchstaben — von null bis zwanzig

paragraphs.text: The box at the top right of this page shows a small trap that catches almost everyone at first: in {{de:vierzehn}} the stress sits on the second half, {{de:zehn}}, while in the answer to a maths problem the number sits where a German expects it. Say the pair aloud and your ear will separate them — {{de:vierZEHN}} against {{de:VIERzig}} — even though the spelling is only a couple of letters apart.

Eleven and twelve refuse the pattern completely: {{de:elf}} and {{de:zwölf}} are their own words, with no {{de:zehn}} hiding inside them. From thirteen upward the pattern is honest — the unit comes first and {{de:zehn}} follows — until twenty, where {{de:zwanzig}} closes the set and the {{de:-zig}} you have just met returns whenever you go on to thirty.
elf · zwölf · dreizehn · vierzehn · fünfzehn · sechzehn · siebzehn · achtzehn · neunzehn · zwanzig

Two spellings in that line are worth a second glance: {{de:sechzehn}} drops the t of {{de:sechs}}, and {{de:siebzehn}} drops the en of {{de:sieben}}. Both changes exist to keep the word short enough to say quickly, and both are written for you on the number line above.

paragraphs.text: On a telephone you will not catch every number, and a German speaker will not catch every word you say. This page hands you the four sentences that keep the conversation alive when that happens. They are more useful than any single word in the lesson, because they buy you time without ending the call.
Wie bitte? · Entschuldigung, noch einmal bitte. · Das verstehe ich nicht. · Bitte ein bisschen langsamer.

Say them without apology. Native speakers use exactly the same four lines with each other, and {{de:Wie bitte?}} in particular is a perfectly polite, perfectly normal reply to anything you did not hear.

blocks.prompt: How do you say the @ sign aloud?
blocks.explanationEnglish: The symbol is called ät, so the address runs alexis unterstrich barbos ät quinnet Punkt com.

concept.title: Zeichen einer E-Mail-Adresse
concept.rule: Spoken German names each symbol instead of reading it: @ is ät, the full stop is Punkt, the hyphen is minus and the underscore is Unterstrich.
concept.exampleGerman: alexis_barbos@quinnet.com — alexis unterstrich barbos ät quinnet Punkt com
concept.exampleEnglish: alexis_barbos@quinnet.com read aloud, symbol by symbol.
